## Original problem

What happens to information about the physical state of matter that forms a black hole when the black hole evaporates?

BODY
The account, objection, and rival each converge on a stance and then diverge on what remains load-bearing. I want to separate three things they braid together, and say which I take up.

First, the shared move. All three decline to answer the original problem and all three treat the trivialization-versus-relocation dispute as the live site. The account narrows to the revision condition on the conditional. The objection presses that the narrowing may exclude the original question. The rival proposes replacing 'correlation recovery' with 'joint-state consistency' as the frame. I accept the shared refusal to answer, and I accept that the frame is itself contestable. What I do not accept is that these are three independent proposals. The rival's reframing, if it succeeds, does not sit alongside the account's conditional; it displaces it. So the choice between them is not additive.

Second, the double-trivialization point. The account says it will not count the double result as a defect absent a bridge about what the two tests share. The objection says the result is inert absent that bridge. These are not the same. 'Not a defect' leaves it as a datum with unassigned significance; 'inert' assigns it zero significance. I side with the weaker claim, because inertness is itself a substantive verdict about the result's bearing, and no one has argued that the stipulation of distinctness exhausts every possible shared quantity. The stronger claim overreaches in the direction opposite to the defect claim it is meant to correct.

Third, the rival's gauge-choice analogy. This is the most interesting move and the least defended. The rival itself flags the obvious objection: gauge choices are supposed to be physically inert, while trivialization and relocation are supposed to mark distinguishable failures. If the analogy holds, the original dispute loses its subject matter. If it fails, the rival has merely renamed the dispute. The rival concedes the objection is live and does not resolve it. I treat the analogy as a hypothesis with a specified defeat condition, not as a reframing.

On attribution, I extend the caution further than either the account or the rival does. The account calls its own 'defect-detector' gloss a reading. The rival calls 'trivialization' potentially rhetorical. Both are right, and the same caution applies to 'the revision condition' and 'the conditional' as used across all three texts. Those are names for something none of the three authors has quoted. The absence of the origin and amend texts is evidence about visibility, not about content; but it is also evidence about the warrants available to me, and I will not treat any of these framings as the text's own until I can see it.

The rival's 'joint consistency' target is a genuine addition because it supplies what the account admits is missing: a candidate for what the diagnostic is a diagnostic of. I do not know whether that candidate is the right one, and the rival does not claim it is. But it has the property the account's target lacks, namely that it is specifiable without presupposing the answer. That is a reason to work on it, not a reason to adopt it.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up, I commit to keeping the account's revision condition and the rival's joint-consistency target as competing frames rather than as complementary tools, and to treating any attempt to combine them as owing an argument for why the combination does not collapse one into the other.

On double-trivialization I hold the weaker line: I will not count the result as a defect, but I will not call it inert either, because inertness is a verdict nobody has earned. If someone supplies a bridge about what the two tests share, that bridge bears on both my position and the objection's.

On the gauge-choice analogy I treat it as a hypothesis. Its defeat condition is the objection the rival already names: that gauge choices are physically inert while the two failures are supposed to be distinguishable. If someone shows the analogy cannot survive that, I drop the analogy rather than the dispute.

My attribution caution runs against my own use of 'the conditional' and 'the revision condition' as though these named something I have seen. I will not attribute to the origin or amend texts any specific content about the heuristic or the conditional until those texts are visible; visibility is what would settle it, and its absence is not evidence about what they say.

I am not answering the original problem, not asserting anything about Hawking radiation or the horizon, and not treating the narrowed dispute as exhausting what the original question asked. Nothing here is a truth certificate about the physics, or about which of these three framings the texts actually support.

BODY
The problem — what happens to information about the physical state of matter that formed a black hole when the black hole evaporates — currently sits unresolved across this material. What I can see is a layered disagreement about how to pose it, and I want to state the layers rather than pick among them.

The join's view is a comparative one: it holds that the body_return and the commitment_return agree that the cross's precision demand is genuine but that the cross's dissolution corollary is not supported. Whether that agreement is itself a good reading of the two continuations is not something the material settles. The join also reports a fork about test design. The body_return, as the join reads it, proposes testing whether the Page curve can be derived without presupposing a sharp horizon or a well-defined radiation entropy. The commitment_return, as the join reads it, replaces this with a weaker test: whether the curve's derivation presupposes a semiclassical matter sector on a fixed or slowly evolving background. The join explicitly declines to adjudicate between them.

The cross's own commitments present a different stance: that body_route and commitment_route are competing framings rather than competing answers, and that the disagreement is about what the question presupposes. The cross identifies shared assumptions — unitary gravitational evolution, thermal-looking evaporation, the horizon as a meaningful boundary, the Page curve as a unitarity diagnostic — and asserts that these are load-bearing in both accounts and undefended in either. The cross's proposed next move is to specify what 'information about the physical state' means (amplitudes, entanglement correlations, or coarse classical summary), and to check whether the conflict survives that specification. The cross also attaches a conditional: if the Page curve can be derived without presupposing a sharp horizon or well-defined radiation entropy, the commitment_route's worry weakens; if not, the body_route's confidence that the problem is well posed is doing more work than its premises support.

The join's commitments then treat the cross's shared-assumption reading as possibly the cross's own synthesis rather than a settled reading of body_route, and flag that if that attribution is wrong, the join's asymmetry argument loses its main support. So the join is authored with an explicit vulnerability: it depends on an attribution to a route whose own text is not visible here.

What I take from this for the present node: there is a real disagreement about the right diagnostic, but the material does not adjudicate it, and the adjudication would depend on a textual question — what body_route actually held — that is not available in this view. I do not answer the original question. I do not treat the cross's shared-assumption synthesis or the join's asymmetry claim as established. I do not treat the body_return's derivability test and the commitment_return's presupposition test as interchangeable. I note that the cross's selected view here is commitments only; its body is not visible in this invocation, so I cannot check the cross's own framing against its body text, and I do not treat that absence as evidence about what the cross's body said.

A substantive point I will surface without resolving: the two tests target different things. The derivability test asks whether a particular quantity can be obtained under weakened horizon and entropy presuppositions. The presupposition test asks whether the derivation requires a background assumption about the matter sector. A 'yes' to one does not entail a 'no' to the other. Conflating them would be a mistake the material does not commit. But whether either is the right diagnostic for the underlying question is exactly what is in dispute, and the join is honest that it does not settle it.

On the physics itself, nothing in this material gives a mechanism or an answer. The conditional — unitary global evolution plus a smooth locally empty horizon precluding the initial microstate from being carried in observably accessible outgoing correlations for an outside observer requiring both — appears in both the join and the cross in different roles: the join's commitments treat it as a proposed locus, the cross treats some of its ingredients as shared undefended assumptions. That role difference is itself part of what the join records.
COMMITMENTS
Taking this up commits me to holding the comparative structure of the join as the object of attention, not as a verdict about the physics. That means I keep the body_return's derivability test and the commitment_return's presupposition test distinct, and I do not treat either as having been run or as having a known outcome; the material supplies no derivation.

I take on the claim that the cross's shared-assumption reading is a candidate reading of the routes rather than a settled one, and that if that attribution is wrong, the join's asymmetry argument loses its main support. This is a conditional commitment, not a claim that the attribution is in fact wrong. I am not treating the absence of an origin text in this invocation as evidence about what any earlier route held.

I hold the conditional about unitary evolution plus a smooth horizon as a proposed locus, not as an established premise. I do not assert it. A demonstration that a relational or coarse-grained measure makes the conditional trivially satisfiable — rather than merely relocating which quantity is at issue — would weaken the framing of it as the residual tension, and I would revise accordingly.

The cross's proposed specification of 'information' (amplitudes, entanglement correlations, coarse classical summary) is a proposed move I leave open; I do not commit to a prediction about whether specification will dissolve the tension or leave it intact, and I do not commit to the cross's conditional that says a successful Page-curve derivation under weakened presuppositions would weaken the commitment_route's worry, since that conditional depends on the precision-demand framing I am not taking as settled.

Three things I explicitly do not commit to: that any route's menu of mechanisms is exhaustive; that semiclassical Hawking radiation has been shown featureless in the correlation structure relevant to the microstate; and that the horizon must remain smooth on all proposals.

I propose no adjudication of the underlying physics and no answer to the original question. What I take up is the map — where the continuations are said to agree, where they diverge on test design, and which attributed premises carry the weight — and that map is provisional and stands or falls with the correctness of its attributions. If the cross's body, or the body_route, or any earlier origin text becomes visible and contradicts the attributions relied on here, this node should be revised rather than defended.
